1 Tablespoon Sugar to Grams Converter

Convert US tablespoons of sugar into grams — accurate for granulated, brown, and powdered sugar.

Gram Equivalent:

12.5 grams (12.5 g)

*Granulated sugar: 1 cup = 200g, 1 tbsp = 1/16 cup. Packed brown sugar ≈ 13.8g/tbsp. Powdered sugar ≈ 7.5g/tbsp.

How Many Grams in 1 Tablespoon of Sugar?

1 US tablespoon of granulated white sugar equals 12.5 grams. This is based on the standard density of 200g per US cup ÷ 16 tablespoons. But sugar type matters: brown sugar (packed) weighs about 13.8g per tablespoon, while powdered sugar weighs only about 7.5g per tablespoon.

The Conversion Formula (Tbsp → Grams)

  • Grams = Tablespoons × (Grams-per-Cup ÷ 16)
  • Granulated Sugar: 1 tbsp × (200 ÷ 16) = 12.5 grams
  • Brown Sugar (packed): 1 tbsp × (220 ÷ 16) = 13.8 grams
  • Powdered Sugar: 1 tbsp × (120 ÷ 16) = 7.5 grams

Packed vs Unpacked Brown Sugar

Most American recipes that call for brown sugar mean packed brown sugar — pressed firmly into the measuring cup or spoon until it holds its shape when turned out. Packed brown sugar weighs about 13.8g per tablespoon (220g/cup). The same volume of loose brown sugar weighs about 12.5g per tablespoon — a 10% difference. When in doubt, pack it: that's what recipe writers almost always intend.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: How many grams is 1 tablespoon of granulated sugar?

A1: One US tablespoon of granulated white sugar weighs 12.5 grams, based on the standard density of 200g per US cup ÷ 16 tablespoons.

Q2: Does brown sugar weigh more than white sugar per tablespoon?

A2: When packed (as most recipes intend), yes — about 13.8g per tablespoon vs 12.5g for granulated. The molasses in brown sugar adds weight, and the packing eliminates air pockets. Loose brown sugar weighs roughly the same as white sugar.

Q3: How many grams is 1 tablespoon of powdered sugar?

A3: One US tablespoon of powdered (confectioners') sugar weighs approximately 7.5 grams. It is much lighter than granulated sugar — nearly half the weight per tablespoon — because the fine, aerated particles trap air.
